# 053 · An idiv that leaves division by zero to the host, proved to throw exactly there

[← All examples](../README.md)

| Verdict | Categories | Severity if shipped | Change | Verified unit | Approach |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **✓ Verified: property holds on every input** | functional, no-false-positive | none | cleanup, behaviour change not intended | [`Arithmetic#idiv`](../../examples/apps/mica/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/mica/interp/Arithmetic.java) | [B11: Property proofs](../../lib/README.md) |

> The interpreter's `idiv` checks for a zero divisor and throws `ArithmeticException` before dividing on the host. A developer notices that the host is itself a JVM, whose division throws the same exception on the same input, and removes the check from `idiv` and `irem`. The property committed for each kernel now declares the exceptional behaviour as JML does, `throws: ArithmeticException when divisor == 0`, instead of assuming the zero divisor away; the prover covers the exceptional path with the normal one and proves that the host throws exactly where the check did.

Tags: [jvm-internals](../README.md#tag-jvm-internals), [interpreter-semantics](../README.md#tag-interpreter-semantics), [special-values](../README.md#tag-special-values), [exceptions](../README.md#tag-exceptions), [throws-clause](../README.md#tag-throws-clause)

## The change

Remove the explicit zero check from `idiv` and `irem` and return `dividend / divisor` and `dividend % divisor` directly; the comment says that the host's own `idiv` throws the `ArithmeticException` the instruction requires. The tests for rounding, the sign of the remainder, the division identity and division by zero pass.

**Before** ([`Arithmetic.java`](../../examples/apps/mica/src/main/java/net/terminalvalue/mica/interp/Arithmetic.java), line 11):

```java
    private Arithmetic() {}

    /**
     * {@code idiv}: the quotient rounded towards zero. Division by zero throws {@code ArithmeticException}.
     * The one overflow, {@code Integer.MIN_VALUE / -1}, is specified: the result is the dividend, and no
     * exception is thrown.
     */
    public static int idiv(int dividend, int divisor) {
        if (divisor == 0) {
            throw new ArithmeticException("/ by zero");
        }
        return dividend / divisor;
    }

    /** {@code irem}: the remainder, with the sign of the dividend, so that {@code (a / b) * b + (a % b) == a}. */
    public static int irem(int dividend, int divisor) {
        if (divisor == 0) {
            throw new ArithmeticException("/ by zero");
        }
        return dividend % divisor;
    }
}
```

**After:**

```java
    private Arithmetic() {}

    /**
     * {@code idiv}: the quotient rounded towards zero. Division by zero throws {@code ArithmeticException}, which
     * is what the host's own {@code idiv} throws, so the kernel does not check first. The one overflow,
     * {@code Integer.MIN_VALUE / -1}, is specified: the result is the dividend, and no exception is thrown.
     */
    public static int idiv(int dividend, int divisor) {
        return dividend / divisor;
    }

    /** {@code irem}: the remainder, with the sign of the dividend, so that {@code (a / b) * b + (a % b) == a}. */
    public static int irem(int dividend, int divisor) {
        return dividend % divisor;
    }
}
```

## What the verifier found

The method returns without throwing and `(divisor != -1 || result == -dividend) && (divisor != 1 || result == dividend)` holds on every input, and throws `java.lang.ArithmeticException` exactly when `divisor == 0`.

This is a proof over the whole domain (dividend: int × divisor: int), not a sample. JBMC turned the statement into a satisfiability problem over the bytecode and showed that it has no solution: no input violates the property.

## Would the existing tests have caught it?

Every existing unit test passes, as it should (`java -ea net.terminalvalue.mica.Tests`, run against the patched code).

## Why it matters

Whether a check is redundant depends on what the code under it does on the inputs the check excluded, and a reviewer reading `dividend / divisor` has to know that Java's `/` throws `ArithmeticException` on zero (it does), that it throws nothing on `Integer.MIN_VALUE / -1` (it does not; JLS §15.17.2), and that the exception's class is the one the guest program's `catch` will name (it is). A port of this kernel to a host whose division traps, or returns an unspecified value, would make the same cleanup a silent miscompilation of every guest program that catches `/ by zero`. The tests cover division by zero with one input each for `idiv` and `irem`.

## Why the verdict is right

Until this change the property of `idiv` was stated under `assume: divisor != 0`, which is the usual way to keep an exception out of a property and leaves the exceptional path to the tests. The property now has a throws clause, `throws: ArithmeticException when divisor == 0`, JML's `signals`: on the inputs where the condition holds the method must throw that exception, and everywhere else it must return and the assertion must hold. The tool compiles the clause into the generated harness as a handler for the declared class, caught before the generic ones, and an `expected` flag computed before the call, and asserts that the two agree; JBMC proves both paths of the patched `idiv` in a fraction of a second, as it does `irem`. The proof says what the reviewer had to know: the host's division throws exactly on zero, an `ArithmeticException` and not a subclass of something else, and on `Integer.MIN_VALUE / -1` it returns the dividend, which the assertion's `divisor != -1 || result == -dividend` still pins down. The exceptional path is no longer assumed away: a future `idiv` that throws on some other input, or returns on zero, fails the same property.

## What to do

Merge. The throws clause stays as the kernel's specification of its exceptional behaviour, in the file the build proves; the tests for division by zero stay as documentation, and no longer carry the check alone.

## Notes

- The throws clause of the property brings the exceptional path under the proof.
- Leaving division by zero to the host throws exactly where the removed check did. Compare 034, the unsafe change on the same method.

<details><summary>The statement the prover checked (generated harness)</summary>

```java
/** Generated by jvmcontract: asserts a property of a method on every input. The class file JBMC checks is generated directly; this is the same statement, for readers. */
public final class PropertyHarness {
    public static void check(int dividend, int divisor) {
        int result = 0;
        int e = 0;
        int expected = 0; // the throws clause that applies: the first whose condition holds
        if (divisor == 0) { expected = 1; } // java.lang.ArithmeticException
        try { result = net.terminalvalue.mica.interp.Arithmetic.idiv(dividend, divisor); } catch (java.lang.ArithmeticException t) { e = -1; } catch (java.lang.NumberFormatException t) { e = 1; } catch (java.lang.ArithmeticException t) { e = 2; } catch (java.lang.NullPointerException t) { e = 3; } catch (java.lang.ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException t) { e = 4; } catch (java.lang.StringIndexOutOfBoundsException t) { e = 5; } catch (java.lang.IndexOutOfBoundsException t) { e = 6; } catch (java.lang.NegativeArraySizeException t) { e = 7; } catch (java.lang.ClassCastException t) { e = 8; } catch (java.lang.IllegalStateException t) { e = 9; } catch (java.lang.IllegalArgumentException t) { e = 10; } catch (java.lang.UnsupportedOperationException t) { e = 11; } catch (java.util.NoSuchElementException t) { e = 12; } catch (java.util.ConcurrentModificationException t) { e = 13; } catch (java.lang.RuntimeException t) { e = 14; } catch (java.lang.Error t) { e = 15; }
        assert expected != 0 ? e == -expected : e == 0 && ((divisor != -1 || result == -dividend) && (divisor != 1 || result == dividend)); // the declared exception where its condition holds; elsewhere no exception, and the property
    }
}
```
